extracted.intended_audience: natural philosophers / physicists and experimentalists studying pendulum motion and fluid resistance (readers of Newton's Principia)
extracted.subtask_description: The page gives theoretical propositions, corollaries and detailed experiments for determining how fluid resistance depends on velocity, body size and fluid density, and for measuring that resistance using pendulum oscillations. It also gives scaling laws for dynamical similarity of particle systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Si resistentia sit ut velocitas, figura B K Ta ellipsis erit quam proxime.
rubrics_metrics.description: Original: "Si resistentia sit ut velocitas, figura B K Ta ellipsis erit quam proxime."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the resisting force of the medium is proportional to the instantaneous velocity, then the locus of motion (figure B K Ta) is approximately an ellipse. The text justifies this by comparing velocities in the resistant medium to velocities in a non-resistant medium and by constructing an ellipse with semiaxes given by those characteristic quantities; areas/rectangles representing work or retardation are equated to show the geometrical approximation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Si resistentia sit in duplicata ratione velocitatis, figura B K V Ta fere parabola erit.
rubrics_metrics.description: Original: "Quod si resistentia D K sit in duplicata ratione velocitatis, figura B K V Ta fere parabola erit..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If resistance is proportional to the square of the velocity, then the path (figure B K V Ta) is approximately a parabola (vertex V, axis O F). The passage shows that the corresponding area/rectangle relations lead to this parabola approximation and links the geometric construction to the relation between resistance and pendulum length.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propositio XXXI — difference of descent and ascent arcs scales with resistance
rubrics_metrics.description: Original: "Si corporis oscillantis resistentia in singulis arcium descriptorum partibus proportionaliter augeatur vel diminutatur in data ratione; differentia inter arcum descensu descriptum & arcum subsequente ascensu descriptum, augebitur vel diminuetur in eadem ratione."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The difference between the arc described in descent and the subsequent ascent (the loss per oscillation) arises from the retardation due to the resisting medium, and thus scales in the same ratio as any prescribed change in the resisting force applied to corresponding arc elements. Practically, altering resistance locally by a given factor changes the arc-difference by the same factor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corol. I to Prop. XXXI — linear law (resistance ∝ velocity) implies arc-difference ∝ total arc
rubrics_metrics.description: Original: "Unde si resistentia sit ut velocitas, differentia arcuum in eodem medio erit ut arcus totus descriptus : & contra."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If resistance is proportional to velocity, then the decrement (difference between descent and subsequent ascent arcs) is proportional to the total arc described; conversely, observing that arc-difference scales with total arc suggests resistance ∝ velocity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corol. II to Prop. XXXI — quadratic law (resistance ∝ v^2) implies arc-difference ∝ (total arc)^2
rubrics_metrics.description: Original: "Si resistentia sit in duplicata ratione velocitatis, differentia illa erit in duplicata ratione arcus totius : & contra."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If resistance ∝ v^2, the arc-loss per oscillation is (approximately) proportional to the square of the total arc; conversely, a squared dependence of arc-loss on total arc indicates v^2 dependence of resistance.

rubrics_metrics.name: General corollary on arbitrary power laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Original: "Et universaliter, si resistentia sit in triplicata vel alia quavis ratione velocitatis, differentia erit in eadem ratione arcus totius : & contra."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: More generally, if resistance scales as any power of velocity, the arc-difference scales with the corresponding power of the total arc. This provides a general diagnostic: measure how arc-loss scales with arc size to infer the velocity-dependence of resistance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corol. 4 — mixed dependence decomposes additively in arc-differences
rubrics_metrics.description: Original: "Et si resistentia sit partim in ratione simplici velocitatis, partim in ejusdem ratione duplicata, differentia erit partim in ratione arcus totius & partim in ejus ratione duplicata : & contra."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If resistance has multiple components (e.g., a term ∝ v and a term ∝ v^2), then the observed arc-difference is the sum of contributions each following the corresponding power-law dependence; thus one can separate components by observing the functional dependence on arc size or velocity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using pendulum oscillations to determine medium resistance (Scholium General)
rubrics_metrics.description: Original: "Ex his propositionibus, per oscillationes pendulorum in mediis quibuscunque, invenire licet resistentiam mediorum."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure: mark a point on the pendulum's string, measure arcs described on descent and final ascent, count number of oscillations required for the pendulum to lose a specified fraction of its motion (e.g., an eighth or a quarter). From counts over different initial arcs and known pendulum geometry, infer how arc-difference depends on velocity and thereby deduce the law of resistance (linear, quadratic, etc.). The author gives detailed experimental setups (wooden and leaden spheres, distances, lengths, measured arc sizes in 'digits') and shows how to reduce observations analytically to coefficients of polynomial dependence on V.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data-model: express arc-difference as polynomial in maximum velocity (A V + B V^2 + C V^3 ...)
rubrics_metrics.description: Original: "Designet jam V velocitatem maximam ... fingamus quod differentia arcuum sit AV + BV^2 + CV^3."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fit coefficients A, B, C by selecting oscillation observations where maximal velocities are in known ratios (e.g., 1, 4, 16 for halved/doubled/quadrupled arcs in reduced-to-cycloid reasoning) and solving the resulting linear system. Use the fitted polynomial to derive resistance as a function of V and then normalize by the pendulum length and the body's weight to obtain resistance per unit weight or per unit length.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental measurement details and controls
rubrics_metrics.description: Original passages describing: marking a point on the string, placing a graduated rule to note arc lengths in digits, suspending spheres by fine thread from a hook, measuring oscillation counts to specified loss fractions etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key practical points: use a firm suspension hook so the suspension point is effectively fixed; note the distance between suspension and the centre of the bob; use a graduated scale to measure arcs; count oscillations to the specified motion loss (e.g., number of oscillations until one-eighth of motion lost). Account for buoyancy when weighing immersed bodies and correct pendulum effective length when the bob carries fluid weight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determination of resistance components and normalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Original: passages computing numerical coefficients and expressing 'resistentia globi ad ejus pondus ut ... ad longitudinem penduli'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After fitting the velocity-dependence polynomial, express the resisting force relative to the bob's weight and to the pendulum length between suspension and center. Use these normalized ratios to compare resistance across different experiments and to convert arc-differences into equivalent resisting-force measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scaling law for similarly moving bodies: resistance scales with square of diameter (approx.) for equal velocities
rubrics_metrics.description: Original: "Ergo resistentiae globorum aequivelocium erant in minore ratione quam duplicata diametrorum... dico quod resistentiae globorum ... in duplicata ratione diametrorum."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From experiments with wooden and leaden spheres of different diameters, after subtracting internal frictional contributions, the author finds that resistance for equal velocities is approximately proportional to the square of the diameter (i.e., resistance ∝ diameter^2), and for bodies of equal size and velocity, resistance ∝ velocity^2 (when that component dominates). This is supported by comparisons of measured coefficients and geometric arguments about cross-sectional areas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fluid-density proportionality: resistance ∝ fluid density (for rapidly moving bodies)
rubrics_metrics.description: Original: "...resistentiam corporum celeriter motorum densitati fluidorum in quibus moventur proportionalem esse quam proxime."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experiments comparing oscillations in air, water and mercury indicate that for bodies moving sufficiently fast, the part of resistance proportional to v^2 scales approximately with the density of the fluid. The author reports ratios (e.g., resistance in mercury : water : air approximating their densities) and notes deviations when container geometry or viscosity effects intervene.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caveat: container-wall and viscosity effects can distort measurements
rubrics_metrics.description: Original: "quod arca nimis angusta esset pro magnitudine globi penduH, & motum aquae cedentis prae angustla sua nimis impediebat."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the vessel or surrounding geometry is too confined relative to the moving body, flow is impeded and observed resistance increases beyond the expected density/size scaling; similarly, more tenacious (viscous) fluids of the same density resist more. Thus experiments must use appropriately large containers and account for fluid viscosity and boundary effects to obtain reliable scaling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal vs external surface resistance (pyxis experiment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Original: long account culminating in: "Est igitur resistentia pyxidis vacuae in partibus internis quinquies millies minor quam ejusdem resistentia in externa superficie, & amplius."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The pyxis (small box) experiment tests whether resistance arises from a subtle pervasive ether penetrating pores (internal resistance) or from action on external surface. The observed result: the resistance attributable to internal parts is negligible (many orders of magnitude smaller) compared to external-surface resistance; hence the dominant resisting action is on the outside surface. Experimental method: compare oscillations of empty and filled box of otherwise identical geometry, correct for added mass/length, ensure firm hook, multiple repeats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental control: ensure fixed suspension point (firm hook)
rubrics_metrics.description: Original: passages noting that an 'uncus infirmus' (weak hook) yielded incorrect results until replaced by a firm hook so the suspension point remained immobile.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A flexible or yielding suspension point biases oscillation counts and apparent resistance (the hook's motion absorbs/returns energy). Use a firm, sharp hook or otherwise ensure the suspension point is effectively fixed to obtain accurate damping/resistance measurements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propositio XXXII — dynamic similitude for similar particle systems
rubrics_metrics.description: Original: "Si corporum systemata duo similia ... & si ... densitatis ad invicem & inter se temporibus proportionalibus similiter moveri incipiant ... dico quod systematum particulae illae pergent inter se temporibus proportionalibus similiter moveri."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If two systems of particles are geometrically similar, composed of proportionally corresponding particles, and have densities/dimensions scaled so that accelerative forces (which are taken as proportional to inverse particle diameter and direct square of velocity) correspond appropriately, then the two systems will evolve similarly with time scaled proportionally. This gives a criterion for dynamical similarity and scaling in mechanical systems: similarity of geometry, particle correspondence, and proportionality of density/time scaling leads to similar motion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propositio XXXIII — composite scaling for resistance of system parts
rubrics_metrics.description: Original: "...dico quod systematum partes majores resistuntur in ratione composita ex duplicata ratione velocitatum suarum & duplicata ratione diametrorum & ratione densitatis partium systematum."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The resistance experienced by larger parts of a system arises partly from centripetal/centrifugal-type internal forces and partly from collisions/reflections; combining these contributions leads to the conclusion that resistance scales (for corresponding parts) proportionally to the square of their velocities, the square of their diameters, and their material densities (i.e., resistance ∝ v^2 * diameter^2 * density). The text justifies this by decomposing sources of resistance and tracing how each contribution scales with the quoted quantities.
